texts.preamble: State Of Gujarat vs M/S Kiran Kirana Store on 6 April, 2015 Author: K.J.Thaker Bench: K.J.Thaker R/Cr.A/51/2003 Judgment In The High Court Of Gujarat At Ahmedabad Criminal Appeal No. 51 of 2003 For Approval And Signature: Honourable Mr.Justice K.J.Thaker ================================================================ 1 Whether Reporters of Local Papers may be allowed to see the judgment ? 2 To be referred to the Reporter or not ? 3 Whether their Lordships wish to see the fair copy of the judgment ? 4 Whether this case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution of India or any order made thereunder ? ================================================================ State Of GUJARAT....Appellant(s) Versus M/S Kiran Kirana Store, & 6....Opponent(s)/Respondent(s) ================================================================ Appearance: Ms Maithili Mehta, App for the Appellant(s) No. 1 Abated for the Opponent(s)/Respondent(s) No. 3 , 5 Mr Muralin Devnani, Advocate for the Opponent(s)/Respondent(s) No. 1-2,4,6-7 ================================================================ Coram: Honourable Mr.Justice K.J.Thaker State Of Gujarat vs M/S Kiran Kirana Store on 6 April, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31092599/ 1 Date : 06/04/2015 Oral Judgment
texts.facts: The brief facts of the prosecution case are as under: 2.1 It is the case of the prosecution that the Food Inspector and complainant Shri Patel Mukesh Amrutlal Sariya visited the shop named M/s. Kiran Kirana Stores situated at Bazar, Sevaliya. During his visit, one partner named Kirankumar Natvarlal Shah i.e. accused no.2 was present there. At that time, he informed that there are two other partners named Shri Natvarlal Shah and Rajeshkumar Natwarlal Shah. In the presence of accused no.1, the Food Inspector had purchased 375 grams groundnut oil from one Lit. groundnut oil of brand of Kiran Brand and paid Rs.17.60 paise for the same. Thereafter, he divided the said sample into three parts and filled in three different bottles after following due R/CR.A/51/2003 JUDGMENT procedure under the Rules and Regulations. Thereafter, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst, at Rajkot along with seal and memorandum on 19.09.1994. The Public Analyst submitted his report on 12.10.1994 to the Local Authority, Nadiad. Thereafter, the Food Inspector - complainant sought for necessary permission to file complaint against the respondents-accused as the report of the Public Analyst, the sample which was found to be adulterated. On these facts, the complaint was filed before the Court, which was numbered as Criminal Case No.413/1995 against the accused. 3. At the time of trial, evidence was led before the Trial Court. The documents were produced and oral evidence of the witnesses were also recorded by the Trial Court and after considering the oral as well as documentary evidence, the learned Magistrate has passed the order of acquittal which is impugned in this appeal. 4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order of acquittal passed by the learned Magistrate Court, the appellant-State has preferred the present Criminal Appeal.
texts.arguments: 5. It was contended by Ms.Maithili Mehta, learned APP for R/CR.A/51/2003 JUDGMENT the appellant-State that the judgment and order of the learned Magistrate Court is not proper, legal and it is erroneous. She has also argued that the learned Magistrate Court has not considered the evidence of the witnesses. She has argued that Food Inspector has followed the Rules prescribed by State Of Gujarat vs M/S Kiran Kirana Store on 6 April, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31092599/ 2 law and he has also followed the procedure of taking the sample and the contents of Form No.6, etc. are just and proper. The sample was seized and sealed properly. Yet, the learned Magistrate Court has not considered the evidence of prosecution. She further submitted that learned Magistrate ought to have appreciated that the permission is the question of fact and is not a question of law. It is the point, which was also not hesitated by the accused in the appeal. She further submitted that the learned Magistrate ought to have considered that the Food Inspector has not committed any breach of Rules 12, 14, 15 and 16 of the Food Adulteration Rules. She further submitted that the learned Magistrate ought to have considered seen that sanction for filing complaint was given by the appropriate authority under the provisions of Section 20 of the Act. She further submitted that the learned Magistrate ought to have considered that the report of the Public Analyst is final and the accused have not exercised their rights/powers under Section 13(2) of the Act and hence, no R/CR.A/51/2003 JUDGMENT prejudice has been caused to the accused and the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt. Therefore, the judgment and order passed by the Magistrate Court requires to be [LEAKAGE_MASK] and [LEAKAGE_MASK] and the present criminal appeal is required to be allowed. 6. As against that, Mr.Muralin Devnani, learned advocate for respondents-original accused supported the judgment and order of the learned Magistrate Court submitting that the same was passed after appreciating the evidence adduced on record by the prosecution and hence, no interference is called for with the same at the hands of this Court. He, therefore, requested that the present criminal appeal is required to be dismissed and the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Magistrate Court is required to be confirmed. 9. It is a settled legal position that in acquittal appeal, the R/CR.A/51/2003 JUDGMENT Appellate Court is not required to re-write the judgment or to give fresh reasonings when the Appellate Court is in agreement with the reasons assigned by the Trial Court acquitting the accused. 10. Even in a recent decision of the Apex Court in the case of State of Goa V. Sanjay Thakran & Anr. In Para-16 of the said decision the Court has observed as under: "16. State Of Gujarat vs M/S Kiran Kirana Store on 6 April, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31092599/ 3 Similar principle has been laid down by the Apex Court in the cases of State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Ram Veer Singh & Ors, reported in 2007 AIR SCW 5553 and in Girja Prasad (Dead) by LRs Vs. state of MP, reported in 2007 AIR SCW 5589. Thus, the powers which this Court may exercise against an order of acquittal are well settled. 12. It is also a settled legal position that in acquittal appeal, the Appellate Court is not required to re-write the judgment or to give fresh reasonings, when the reasons assigned by the Court below are found to be just and proper. Such principle is laid down by the Apex Court in the case of State of Karnataka Vs. Hemareddy, reported in AIR 1981 SC 1417, wherein, it is held as under: "... This court has observed in Girija Nandini Devi V. Bigendra Nandini Chaudhary (1967)1 SCR 93: (AIR 1967 SC 1124) that it is not the duty of the appellate court when it agrees with the view of the trial court on the evidence to repeat the narration of the evidence or to reiterate the reasons given by the trial court expression of general agreement with the reasons given by the Court the decision of which is under appeal, will ordinarily suffice." 15. Learned APP is not in a position to show any evidence to take a contrary view of the matter or that the approach of the learned Magistrate Court is vitiated by some manifest illegality or that the decision is perverse or that the learned Magistrate R/CR.A/51/2003 JUDGMENT Court has ignored State Of Gujarat vs M/S Kiran Kirana Store on 6 April, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31092599/ 4 the material evidence on record.
